title: Adjectives and adverbs: describing things and actions
summary: Choose adjectives to describe people and things and adverbs to explain how actions happen. Form common -ly adverbs, recognise adjectives ending in -ly, and use adverbs to modify adjectives, other adverbs and past participles.
learningObjectives: Form regular -ly adverbs and apply frequent spelling changes such as happy to happily.
Choose adjectives before nouns and adverbs to describe actions, including cases with a verb and its object.
Use adjectives after be, look, feel and sound when describing the subject rather than an action.
Use adverbs to modify adjectives, other adverbs and past participles without changing the intended meaning.
Recognise that words such as friendly and lovely are adjectives despite their -ly ending.

explanation.heading: Form many adverbs with -ly
explanation.body: Many adverbs of manner are built from an adjective plus -ly: careful becomes carefully, sudden becomes suddenly, and serious becomes seriously. Some spellings change: happy becomes happily, easy becomes easily, and terrible becomes terribly. These adverbs commonly describe how an action happens. Not every adverb follows this pattern.
explanation.example: The assistant answered the difficult question patiently.

explanation.heading: Adjectives tell us about nouns
explanation.body: An adjective describes a person, object, place or other noun. It commonly stands before the noun, as in a quiet street or an urgent message. An adverb ending in -ly is generally unsuitable in the same position: a carefully driver is incorrect, but a careful driver is correct. Choose the form according to what is being described.
explanation.example: Our neighbour is a thoughtful listener.

explanation.heading: Adverbs describe actions
explanation.body: To say how someone performs an action or how an event unfolds, use an adverb: the cyclist turned sharply or she described the idea clearly. An adverb can come after the object of a verb, as in she handled the request politely. Do not use the adjective in place of the adverb when the task is describing the manner of the action.
explanation.example: The technician checked every connection thoroughly.

explanation.heading: Linking verbs take adjectives
explanation.body: Be, look, feel, sound, taste and similar verbs can connect a subject to its condition or quality. In this use, an adjective follows: the room looks clean and the students feel nervous. Compare that with an action, as in the cleaners worked carefully. The adjective says what the subject is like; the adverb says how the action is performed.
explanation.example: The instructions seem clear, but the trainee reads them slowly.

explanation.heading: Adverbs can modify more than verbs
explanation.body: Adverbs also intensify or qualify an adjective, another adverb or a past participle. In remarkably useful, remarkably modifies the adjective useful. In surprisingly quickly, surprisingly modifies the adverb quickly. In carefully planned, carefully modifies the participle planned. These phrases can express degree, manner or evaluation rather than describing a separate action.
explanation.example: The proposal was carefully written and surprisingly easy to follow.

explanation.heading: Some -ly words are adjectives
explanation.body: Friendly, lovely, lonely, lively and elderly are adjectives even though they end in -ly. A friendly reply and a lively discussion are normal noun phrases. Do not automatically treat every -ly word as an adverb, and do not invent forms like friendlily when a different natural phrase such as in a friendly way will work better.
explanation.example: We received a friendly welcome at the community centre.

comparisons.title: Adjective describing a noun versus adverb describing an action

left.label: Adjective + noun
left.example: The engineer gave a clear explanation.

right.label: Verb + adverb
right.example: The engineer explained the process clearly.
right.note: Clearly describes how the explaining was done.

left.label: Linking verb + adjective
left.note: Happy describes the children’s state or appearance.

right.label: Action verb + adverb
right.note: Happily describes the manner of waving.

comparisons.title: Adverb modifying adjective versus adverb modifying participle

left.label: Degree + adjective
left.note: Remarkably changes the degree of the adjective light.

right.label: Manner + participle
right.note: Carefully modifies how the device was assembled.

examples.sentence: A friendly receptionist greeted the visitors warmly.
examples.note: Friendly is an adjective describing the receptionist; warmly describes the greeting.

examples.sentence: The speaker gave a confident answer and spoke confidently.
examples.note: Confident describes the answer; confidently describes how the person spoke.

examples.sentence: The sky looked strangely orange at sunset.
examples.note: Strangely modifies the adjective orange; orange describes the sky.

examples.sentence: The team completed the inspection successfully.
examples.note: Successfully describes how the team completed the task.

examples.sentence: The building was badly damaged during the storm.
examples.note: Badly modifies the past participle damaged.

examples.sentence: The music was incredibly loud, and the drummer played incredibly quickly.
examples.note: Incredibly modifies an adjective in the first clause and an adverb in the second.

commonMistakes.why: The word describes a noun, answer, so use the adjective careful.
Slowly describes the manner of completing the repair.
Seem links the subject to a quality, so it needs the adjective happy.
Use the adverb extremely to modify the adjective interesting.
Lovely is already an adjective and can appear directly before evening.

studyTips: Underline the noun or verb you want to describe, then choose the adjective or adverb form accordingly.
Practise common spelling pairs: easy/easily, heavy/heavily, terrible/terribly and happy/happily.
Learn adverb combinations as short phrases: extremely useful, unusually quiet, completely finished and badly damaged.

exercises.prompt: She gave a ___ summary of the meeting.
exercises.feedback: Summary is a noun, so the adjective clear is required.
Carefully is an adverb describing how the guide described the route.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence contains a natural adjective ending in -ly?
exercises.feedback: Lovely is an adjective, so it can describe the noun afternoon.
Felt is a linking verb; nervous describes Maya’s condition.

exercises.prompt: The students answered the questions ___ (confident; write the adverb).
exercises.feedback: Confidently describes the students’ manner of answering.

exercises.prompt: The road became ___ when rain started. (slippery; use the adjective)
exercises.feedback: Became links the road to the adjective slippery, which describes its condition.

exercises.prompt: We finished the task ___ despite the noisy room. (easy; write the -ly adverb only)
exercises.feedback: Easy changes to easily, with y replaced by i, to describe how the task was finished.

exercises.prompt: The report was ___ researched. (thorough; write the adverb only)
Correct only the adjective/adverb form: The instructor spoke very calm during the emergency.
acceptedAnswers: The instructor spoke very calmly during the emergency.
exercises.feedback: Calmly describes how the instructor spoke.

exercises.prompt: Correct only the adjective/adverb form: The exam instructions looked confusingly.
exercises.feedback: Looked links instructions to the adjective confusing.

exercises.prompt: Correct only the adjective/adverb form: That is a beautifully painting.
exercises.feedback: Beautiful is the adjective that describes the noun painting.

exercises.prompt: Correct only the adjective/adverb form: The timetable was complete revised yesterday.
acceptedAnswers: The timetable was completely revised yesterday.
exercises.feedback: Completely is an adverb modifying the past participle revised.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say one sentence using these supplied facts: the dancer / move / graceful / across the stage. Use the past simple and the correct adverb.
acceptedAnswers: The dancer moved gracefully across the stage.
speakingExercises.feedback: Gracefully is the manner adverb modifying moved.

speakingExercises.prompt: Describe a driver, not the way they drive. Begin “He is a” and end “driver”. Use careful.
speakingExercises.feedback: Careful is an adjective describing the driver.

speakingExercises.prompt: The news caused the children to feel excited. Say one complete sentence beginning “The children” and ending “excited”. Use looked as a linking verb.
speakingExercises.feedback: Looked is followed by the adjective excited to describe their appearance.

speakingExercises.prompt: A colleague asks how Zoe explained the plan. The explanation was clear. Reply with one sentence beginning “Zoe explained” and using clearly.
speakingExercises.feedback: Clearly describes Zoe’s way of explaining.

speakingExercises.prompt: Correct only the adjective/adverb form and speak the full sentence: “It was a strangely experience.”
speakingExercises.feedback: Strange is the adjective that describes experience.

speakingExercises.prompt: Use an adverb to strengthen the adjective “helpful”. Begin “The advice was” and say extremely helpful.
Produce exactly two past-simple sentences using these facts. First: the exam / be / difficult. Second: the students / work / carefully. Start each sentence with its subject.
acceptedAnswers: The exam was difficult. The students worked carefully.
speakingExercises.feedback: Difficult describes the exam; carefully describes how the students worked.

speakingExercises.prompt: Describe a document that received careful preparation. Begin “The document was” and end “prepared”. Use carefully as an adverb.
speakingExercises.feedback: Carefully modifies prepared, describing the manner of preparation.

listeningExercises.audioText: The new assistant spoke clearly, but the instructions themselves were confusing.
listeningExercises.prompt: Which part was difficult to understand?
choices: Both the speech and instructions were clear.
listeningExercises.feedback: Clearly describes the manner of speaking, while confusing describes the instructions.

listeningExercises.audioText: The path looked safe, so we walked along it slowly to avoid slipping.
listeningExercises.prompt: How did the group move along the path?
listeningExercises.feedback: Slowly describes how the group walked, even though the path appeared safe.

listeningExercises.audioText: The technician tested the sensors carefully before restarting the machine.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the single adverb immediately after “sensors”.
listeningExercises.feedback: Carefully describes how the sensors were tested.

listeningExercises.audioText: It was a surprisingly easy exercise, and the whole class finished it quickly.
listeningExercises.prompt: What does the speaker say about the exercise?
choices: It was unfinished when time ran out.
listeningExercises.feedback: Surprisingly easy signals that the exercise was easier than expected.

listeningExercises.audioText: Our guests were friendly, and they thanked the volunteers warmly at the end.
listeningExercises.prompt: Which statement is supported by the recording?
choices: The guests were unfriendly but spoke politely.
The volunteers thanked the guests reluctantly.
The guests were kind and expressed their thanks warmly.
listeningExercises.feedback: Friendly describes the guests; warmly describes the way they thanked the volunteers.

listeningExercises.audioText: The report was badly organised, although the data had been carefully collected.
listeningExercises.prompt: What contrast does the speaker make?
choices: Both the structure and data collection were poor.
The data collection was careful, but the report structure was poor.
The report was clearly organised, but the data were missing.
listeningExercises.feedback: Badly organised contrasts with carefully collected.

listeningExercises.audioText: The children felt happy after the performance and walked home cheerfully.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the single adjective immediately after “felt”.
listeningExercises.feedback: Happy describes the children’s state after the linking verb felt.

listeningExercises.audioText: The room was unusually quiet when the meeting began.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two-word adverb and adjective phrase immediately after “was”.
listeningExercises.feedback: Unusually modifies the adjective quiet rather than describing a separate action.
